# 1 Samuel Chapter 17 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 179r-180v | **Source Image:** 1SA_017_page_001.jpg, 1SA_017_page_002.jpg, 1SA_017_page_003.jpg, 1SA_017_page_004.jpg

---

**1** The Philistines gathered their forces for war. They assembled at Socoh in Judah and camped between Socoh and Azekah, at Ephes-dammim.

**2** Saul and the Israelites assembled, camped in the Valley of Elah, and drew up their battle lines to face the Philistines.

**3** The Philistines held one hill and the Israelites held another, with the valley between them.

**4** A champion came out from the Philistine camp. His name was Goliath, from Gath. He stood over nine feet tall.

**5** He wore a bronze helmet on his head and was dressed in a coat of scale armor. The armor weighed five thousand shekels of bronze.

**6** He had bronze greaves on his legs and a bronze javelin slung between his shoulders.

**7** The shaft of his spear was like a weaver's beam, and the iron point of his spear weighed six hundred shekels. His shield-bearer walked ahead of him.

**8** Goliath stood and shouted to the Israelite ranks, "Why do you come out and form your battle lines? Am I not the Philistine, and are you not Saul's servants? Choose a man and have him come down to me.

**9** If he can fight me and kill me, we will become your servants. But if I overcome him and kill him, you will become our servants and serve us."

**10** Then the Philistine said, "I challenge the ranks of Israel this day! Give me a man and let us fight each other!"

**11** When Saul and all Israel heard the Philistine's words, they were dismayed and deeply afraid.

**12** Now David was the son of that Ephrathite from Bethlehem in Judah named Jesse, who had eight sons. In Saul's day, Jesse was already old and advanced in years.

**13** Jesse's three oldest sons had followed Saul to the war. The names of his three sons who went to battle were Eliab the firstborn, Abinadab the second, and Shammah the third.

**14** David was the youngest. The three oldest followed Saul,

**15** while David went back and forth between Saul's service and tending his father's sheep at Bethlehem.

**16** For forty days the Philistine came forward every morning and evening and took his stand.

**17** One day Jesse said to his son David, "Take this half-bushel of roasted grain and these ten loaves of bread for your brothers, and hurry to their camp.

**18** Also take these ten portions of cheese to the commander of their unit. Find out how your brothers are doing and bring back some proof that they are all right."

**19** Saul and the brothers and all the Israelites were in the Valley of Elah, fighting against the Philistines.

**20** David got up early in the morning, left someone in charge of the sheep, loaded up, and set out as Jesse had instructed him. He arrived at the camp encirclement just as the army was going out to its battle positions, shouting the war cry.

**21** Israel and the Philistines drew up facing each other, army against army.

**22** David left his things with the supply keeper, ran to the battle lines, and greeted his brothers.

**23** While he was talking with them, the champion — the Philistine from Gath named Goliath — stepped out from the Philistine ranks and shouted his usual challenge, and David heard it.

**24** When all the Israelite soldiers saw the man, they ran from him in great fear.

**25** The Israelites had been saying, "Do you see this man who keeps coming out? He comes out to defy Israel. The king will give great wealth to the man who kills him. He will also give him his daughter in marriage and will exempt his father's family from taxes in Israel."

**26** David asked the men standing near him, "What will be done for the man who kills this Philistine and removes this disgrace from Israel? Who is this uncircumcised Philistine that he should defy the armies of the living God?"

**27** The soldiers told him what had been promised, saying, "That is what will be done for the man who kills him."

**28** When David's oldest brother Eliab heard him speaking with the men, he burned with anger at him. "Why have you come down here?" he demanded. "And who did you leave those few sheep with out in the wilderness? I know your arrogance and the wickedness of your heart — you came down just to watch the battle!"

**29** David replied, "What have I done now? Can't I even ask a question?"

**30** He turned away from him to someone else and asked the same thing, and the soldiers gave him the same answer as before.

**31** What David said was overheard and reported to Saul, and Saul sent for him.

**32** David said to Saul, "No one should lose heart because of this Philistine. Your servant will go and fight him."

**33** But Saul said to David, "You cannot go out against this Philistine and fight him. You are only a youth, and he has been a warrior since his boyhood."

**34** David said to Saul, "Your servant has been tending his father's sheep. When a lion or a bear came and carried off a lamb from the flock,

**35** I went after it, struck it down, and rescued the lamb from its mouth. When it turned on me, I grabbed it by the jaw, struck it, and killed it.

**36** Your servant has killed both the lion and the bear. This uncircumcised Philistine will be like one of them, because he has defied the armies of the living God."

**37** David added, "The LORD who rescued me from the paw of the lion and the paw of the bear will rescue me from the hand of this Philistine." Saul said to David, "Go, and the LORD be with you."

**38** Saul dressed David in his own battle tunic. He put a bronze helmet on his head and outfitted him with armor.

**39** David strapped Saul's sword over the tunic and tried walking around, because he was not used to them. David said to Saul, "I cannot go in these. I am not used to them." So he took them off.

**40** He took his staff in his hand, chose five smooth stones from the stream, put them in the pouch of his shepherd's bag, and with his sling in his hand, he approached the Philistine.

**41** Meanwhile, the Philistine kept coming closer to David, with his shield-bearer ahead of him.

**42** When the Philistine looked David over and saw that he was just a youth, ruddy and handsome, he despised him.

**43** The Philistine said to David, "Am I a dog, that you come at me with sticks?" And the Philistine cursed David by his gods.

**44** The Philistine said to David, "Come here, and I will give your flesh to the birds of the sky and the beasts of the field."

**45** David said to the Philistine, "You come against me with a sword, a spear, and a javelin. But I come against you in the name of the LORD of Armies, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied.

**46** This very day the LORD will hand you over to me. I will strike you down and cut off your head. Today I will give the carcasses of the Philistine army to the birds of the sky and the wild animals of the earth, and the whole world will know that there is a God in Israel.

**47** And everyone gathered here will know that the LORD does not save by sword and spear. For the battle belongs to the LORD, and he will hand all of you over to us."

**48** As the Philistine moved closer to attack him, David ran quickly toward the battle line to meet the Philistine.

**49** David reached into his bag, took out a stone, slung it, and struck the Philistine on the forehead. The stone sank into his forehead, and he fell facedown on the ground.

**50** So David triumphed over the Philistine with a sling and a stone. He struck the Philistine down and killed him — without a sword in his hand.

**51** David ran and stood over the Philistine. He grabbed the Philistine's sword, drew it from its sheath, and killed him. Then he cut off his head with it. When the Philistines saw that their champion was dead, they turned and ran.

**52** Then the men of Israel and Judah surged forward with a shout and pursued the Philistines to the entrance of Gath and to the gates of Ekron. Philistine dead lay along the Shaaraim road all the way to Gath and Ekron.

**53** When the Israelites returned from chasing the Philistines, they plundered their camp.

**54** David took the Philistine's head and brought it to Jerusalem, but he kept the Philistine's weapons in his own tent.

**55** When Saul had watched David go out to face the Philistine, he said to Abner, the commander of the army, "Abner, whose son is that young man?" Abner replied, "As surely as you live, Your Majesty, I do not know."

**56** The king said, "Find out whose son this youth is."

**57** As soon as David returned from killing the Philistine, Abner brought him before Saul, with the Philistine's head still in his hand.

**58** Saul asked him, "Whose son are you, young man?" David answered, "I am the son of your servant Jesse of Bethlehem."

---

## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

This is perhaps the most famous chapter in the Hebrew Bible, and its theological architecture is far richer than the popular "underdog" reading suggests. The central declaration -- *ki la-YHVH ha-milchamah* ("the battle belongs to the LORD," v. 47) -- reframes the entire encounter from a contest of warriors to a contest of gods. Goliath's challenge is not merely military; it is theological blasphemy -- he *charaph* ("defies/reproaches") the *ma'arkhoth elohim chayyim* ("armies of the living God," v. 26). David's outrage is not patriotic but doxological.

The armor scene (vv. 38-39) is deeply symbolic. Saul clothes David in his own gear -- literally trying to make the new king fight in the old king's framework. David's refusal ("I am not used to them") is a theological statement: the new thing God is doing cannot be dressed in the old regime's methods. Five smooth stones and a shepherd's sling are the anti-armor, the foolishness of God that is wiser than human wisdom.

The narrator's repeated emphasis on David's youth and beauty (*na'ar admoni*, vv. 42, cf. 16:12) creates deliberate contrast with Goliath's monstrous inventory of bronze and iron (vv. 4-7). The Philistine represents the apex of human military technology; David represents radical dependence on divine power. That the giant falls *facedown* (*al-panav artzah*, v. 49) echoes Dagon falling before the ark (1 Sam 5:3-4) -- the same God topples the same enemy in the same posture.

The tension between chapter 16 (where Saul already knows David) and 17:55-58 (where he asks "whose son is this?") has generated centuries of scholarly discussion. The Leningrad Codex preserves both traditions without harmonization, which is itself a statement: the text trusts the reader to hold complexity.

-- PNEUMA
